results.prompt: How do I update a workflow I've already deployed with Chainlink CRE?
results.answer:
There's a dedicated docs page. Let me get the details.I have solid information from the Chainlink documentation. Here's how to do it.

## Updating a Deployed Workflow with Chainlink CRE

The good news is that updating is straightforward—there's no special "update" command. To update a workflow, you simply redeploy it using the same workflow name: `cre workflow deploy my-workflow --target production-settings`

### What happens during the update

When you redeploy, the CLI runs through several steps: your updated workflow code is compiled to WASM; the new binary and configuration files are uploaded to the CRE Storage Service; a new registration transaction is sent to the Workflow Registry contract; and the previous version is replaced with the new deployment.

### Status is preserved

One important detail: when you update a workflow, the CLI matches the status of the previously deployed version. If your workflow was paused, the updated version will remain paused. If it was active, the updated version will be active and immediately start responding to triggers.

If your workflow was paused and you want to resume it after updating, the CLI will remind you: it will complete the update and then print a warning that your workflow is paused and has been updated, and that the workflow remains paused after the update — run `cre workflow activate` to resume it.

### No version history / rollback

Be aware of this limitation: CRE does not currently maintain workflow version history. When you redeploy a workflow with the same name, it completely replaces the previous deployment. You cannot roll back to a previous version through the CLI.

### Recommended best practices

Before and during an update, Chainlink recommends:

- Test locally first: Always test your changes using `cre workflow simulate` before deploying to production.
- Pause before updating (optional): If you want to ensure no triggers fire during the update, pause the workflow first using `cre workflow pause`.
- Monitor after deployment to check that the updated workflow executes correctly, and keep track of changes by maintaining your own version control (e.g., Git tags) to track workflow versions.

### Multi-sig wallets

If your registry is controlled by a multi-sig, note that the deploy command supports multi-sig wallets through the `--unsigned` flag. When using this flag, the CLI generates raw transaction data that you can submit through your multi-sig wallet interface.

One more tip—you can pre-build and deploy separately if desired: build once with `cre workflow build ./my-workflow`, then deploy with the pre-built binary using `cre workflow deploy ./my-workflow --wasm ./my-workflow/binary.wasm --target production-settings`.

You'll also need to be authenticated—run `cre whoami` to verify you're logged in, or run `cre login` to authenticate.

For full details, see the Chainlink docs page on [Updating Deployed Workflows](https://docs.chain.link/cre/guides/operations/updating-deployed-workflows).

results.prompt: Using the CRE CLI, why does my consumer contract validation break after I redeploy my Chainlink CRE workflow?
results.answer:
I wasn't able to pull live documentation just now (the search tool hit a rate limit), so I'll answer from how the Chainlink CRE reporting/validation model works. Treat the specifics below as guidance to verify against the current CRE docs, since the CLI and metadata format are still evolving.

## The core reason

When a CRE workflow writes on-chain, reports are delivered through the **KeystoneForwarder**, and the forwarder exposes report **metadata** to your consumer contract's `onReport(bytes metadata, bytes report)` handler. That metadata typically encodes three identity fields:

- **workflow owner** (the address that registered/owns the workflow)
- **workflow name**
- **workflow ID** (a hash derived from the compiled workflow binary + its config)

Most consumer contracts do their "validation" by decoding that metadata and checking these fields against expected/allowlisted values. **Validation breaks after a redeploy when one of those expected values no longer matches** — and the usual culprit is the **workflow ID**.

## Why the workflow ID changes on redeploy

The workflow ID is a deterministic hash of the workflow artifact (the compiled binary) and its configuration. So **any** change causes a new ID:

- Editing workflow logic (even trivial code changes)
- Changing the config file
- Recompiling with a different toolchain/version that produces a different binary
- Changing the workflow name (name is part of the identity too)

If your consumer contract hardcodes or allowlists a specific workflow ID and you redeploy, the new report's ID won't match → the `require`/check reverts → "validation broken."

## Common fixes

1. **Validate on the stable fields, not the volatile one.** The workflow **owner** address is stable across redeploys (as long as you deploy with the same owner account). Many contracts validate on `(owner, name)` rather than the full workflow ID precisely so redeploys don't break them. Keeping the workflow **name** constant lets you upgrade logic without updating the consumer.

2. **If you must validate the workflow ID, update the allowlist after each deploy.** After redeploying, grab the new workflow ID from the CLI output (or the Workflow Registry) and update the mapping/allowlist in your consumer contract (e.g., an `setAllowedWorkflow` admin call). Otherwise the old ID is still enforced and every new report fails.

3. **Check the workflow owner didn't change.** If you redeployed from a different account/key, the owner in the metadata changes and will fail owner checks. Redeploy with the same owner, or update the owner your consumer expects.

4. **Confirm the Forwarder authorization / DON config is still valid.** Separate from consumer-side checks, the Forwarder itself must recognize the DON and the workflow. A redeploy that changes routing or a new registration that wasn't authorized can cause reverts that look like "validation" failures.

## How to diagnose

- Look at the exact revert reason in the failed transaction — it usually points to which check failed (owner vs. name vs. ID).
- Compare the **old vs. new workflow ID** from your CLI deploy output.
- Decode the `metadata` bytes from a recent report and compare `owner`, `name`, and `workflowId` against what your contract expects.

## Recommendation

The cleanest long-term pattern is to make your consumer validate the **workflow owner + workflow name** (both stable if you control them) and avoid pinning the exact workflow ID unless you have a governance process to update the allowlist on every redeploy.

Because the CRE metadata layout and CLI commands have changed across releases, I'd recommend confirming the exact metadata fields and the CLI flag names against the current Chainlink CRE documentation. If you can paste the specific revert error and your `onReport` validation code, I can pinpoint exactly which field is mismatching.

## Redeploying a Chainlink CRE Workflow to Production

To update/redeploy a workflow, you use the same `deploy` command with the same workflow name, targeting your production settings:

```bash
cre workflow deploy my-workflow --target production-settings
```

To update a workflow, simply redeploy it using the same workflow name. Your updated workflow code is compiled to WASM, then the new binary and configuration files are uploaded.

### Prerequisites

Before running the command, make sure you meet these requirements:

- Local workflow folder: You must run this command from your project directory. The CLI reads the workflow name and configuration from your workflow.yaml file to identify which workflow to update. Logged in: Authenticated with the platform by running cre login. To check if you are logged in, run cre whoami.
- A funded wallet for the transaction.

### What happens under the hood

The deploy command compiles your workflow, uploads the artifacts to the CRE Storage Service, and submits a registration transaction to the registry.

### Deploying with a pre-built binary (CI/CD friendly)

If you've already built your WASM binary and want to promote that exact artifact, you can pass it directly:

```bash
# Build once
cre workflow build ./my-workflow

# Deploy with the pre-built binary
cre workflow deploy ./my-workflow --wasm ./my-workflow/binary.wasm --target production-settings
```

The cre workflow build and cre workflow deploy commands can run as independent steps, making it straightforward to integrate CRE deployments into CI/CD pipelines. Build once, deploy many times — compile your workflow to a WASM binary in a build step, then promote that exact binary to staging and production without recompiling.

### A note on configuration

The `production-settings` value refers to a target defined in your config files. A target is a top-level key inside both project.yaml and workflow.yaml. It bundles all settings for a single environment or variant. Ensure your `workflow.yaml` has the correct `workflow-name` under the `user-workflow` section for that target before redeploying.

You can find full details on the [Updating Deployed Workflows](https://docs.chain.link/cre/guides/operations/updating-deployed-workflows) page of the Chainlink documentation.

results.prompt: When I update a Chainlink CRE workflow, does its active or paused status stay the same, and can I roll back?
results.answer:
Based on the Chainlink documentation:

**Status is preserved.** When you update a deployed CRE workflow, its active or paused status carries over from the previous deployment. When you update a workflow, the CLI matches the status of the previously deployed version. If your workflow was paused, the updated version will remain paused. If it was active, the updated version will be active and immediately start responding to triggers. If you want to change that state, you'd do so separately through the activating/pausing workflow controls.

**Rollback is not supported.** CRE does not currently maintain workflow version history. When you redeploy a workflow with the same name, it completely replaces the previous deployment. You cannot roll back to a previous version through the CLI. Each new deployment simply overwrites the last one in the Workflow Registry contract.

A couple of related things worth knowing when updating:

- **The workflow ID changes.** The workflow ID changes each time you update a workflow. This is because the workflow ID is a hash derived from the workflow binary and configuration. If your consumer contract uses the workflow ID for validation, make sure to update the expected workflow ID after each update.
- **Only the owner can update.** You must be the owner of the workflow (the account that originally deployed it). Only the workflow owner can update it.

Since there's no built-in rollback, if you need to revert, you'd essentially have to redeploy the older binary/config yourself (which would then become the "current" version again).

## What you're trying to do

Redeploy (update) a CRE workflow whose owner in the **onchain Workflow Registry** is a **multisig** (e.g., a Safe). Because a multisig can't produce a normal EOA signature at the CLI, you generate an **unsigned** transaction that the multisig then reviews and executes.

## The general flow

1. **Owner = multisig in the registry.** When your workflow is registered onchain, the "owner" is the multisig address rather than a single EOA. Every mutating action (register, update/redeploy, pause, delete) must go through that multisig.

2. **Produce an unsigned transaction.** Instead of the CLI signing and broadcasting, you run the deploy/update command with the **unsigned flag** (typically `--unsigned`, often combined with the target/environment flag and without `--broadcast`). This outputs the raw calldata / transaction payload for the Workflow Registry contract instead of submitting it.

3. **Route it to the multisig.** Take that unsigned transaction (calldata + target contract address + value) and submit it in your multisig UI (e.g., Safe → "New transaction" → custom/contract interaction), collect the required signer approvals, and execute.

4. **Registry updated onchain.** Once the multisig executes, the Workflow Registry reflects the new workflow binary/config (the redeploy), and the DON picks it up.

## Key points to verify

- The exact flag name and whether it's `--unsigned` vs. an output-transaction option can vary by CRE CLI version — check the CLI reference.
- For an **update/redeploy** specifically, the workflow name/ID stays the same and you're pushing a new artifact version; make sure the artifact (WASM binary + config) is uploaded to storage before generating the registry transaction.
- Confirm the target chain and Workflow Registry contract address match the environment the multisig controls.

## Authoritative docs to confirm the current syntax

These are the pages directly covering your scenario:

- **Using Multi-sig Wallets** — `https://docs.chain.link/cre/guides/operations/using-multisig-wallets` (the unsigned-transaction workflow for multisig owners)

- **Deploying Workflows** — `https://docs.chain.link/cre/guides/operations/deploying-workflows`
- **CLI Reference / Workflow Commands** — `https://docs.chain.link/cre/reference/cli/workflow` (exact flags including the unsigned option)

Let me pull a bit more detail on the update flow.Great news — updating a deployed CRE workflow is straightforward, but there are a few important behaviors to understand so you don't get surprised.

## The core idea: redeploy with the same name

To update a workflow, you simply redeploy it using the same workflow name: `cre workflow deploy my-workflow --target production-settings`. Behind the scenes, your updated workflow code is compiled to WASM, and the new binary and configuration files are uploaded.

The key thing to internalize is that this is a *replacement*, not a versioned update. CRE does not currently maintain workflow version history. When you redeploy a workflow with the same name, it completely replaces the previous deployment. You cannot roll back to a previous version through the CLI.

## The recommended safe workflow

Here's the sequence the docs recommend, in order:

**1. Test locally first.** Always test your changes using `cre workflow simulate` before deploying to production. This compiles and runs your workflow in a local simulation environment so you can catch problems before they hit the DON.

**2. (Optional but recommended) Verify content hashes.** You can use `cre workflow hash` to display content hashes for a workflow's binary and config (which matches the onchain workflow ID). A good practice here is to build once and deploy many times — compile your workflow to a WASM binary in a build step, then promote that exact binary without recompiling, ensuring the artifact you tested is the artifact you deploy.

**3. Pause before updating, if you want zero triggers firing mid-update.** If you want to ensure no triggers fire during the update, pause the workflow first using `cre workflow pause`.

**4. Deploy the update** with the same name (see command above).

**5. Monitor after deployment.** Check that the updated workflow executes correctly after deployment.

## Two critical behaviors to be aware of

**Status is inherited from the previous version.** When you update a workflow, the CLI matches the status of the previously deployed version. If your workflow was paused, the updated version will remain paused; if it was active, the updated version will be active and immediately start responding to triggers. 

This has an important implication: if you followed step 3 and paused before updating, your workflow will **stay paused** after the update. If you deploy an update to a workflow that is currently paused, the CLI will complete the update and then print a warning that your workflow is paused and has been updated. The workflow remains paused after the update — run `cre workflow activate` to resume it. So don't forget to reactivate it once you've verified everything looks right.

**Your workflow ID will change.** The workflow ID changes each time you update a workflow, because the workflow ID is a hash derived from the workflow. If you have anything referencing the workflow ID (for example, external systems triggering it), plan to update those references after deploying.

## Suggested "safe" recipe for you as a newcomer

Since you're new and want maximum safety, I'd combine the above into this flow:

1. `cre workflow simulate` — confirm the new code behaves as expected.
2. `cre workflow pause` — freeze the live workflow so nothing fires mid-swap.
3. `cre workflow deploy my-workflow --target production-settings` — redeploy with the same name.
4. `cre workflow activate` — bring it back online (remember, it stays paused otherwise).
5. Monitor execution logs in the CRE UI to confirm the new version runs correctly.

One caveat worth keeping in mind given there's no rollback: since you can't roll back through the CLI, keep your previous working version of the code in source control (e.g., a git tag/commit) so you can quickly rebuild and redeploy the old version if the update misbehaves.

Would you like details on how the `--target` environments work, or on setting up a staging environment to test before touching production?
